Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Marta, a 38-year-old community organizer, grew up in a home where her mother’s boyfriend, her primary caregiver from age six to twelve, was the one she both feared and depended on. The worst incident she can now summon—though it comes not as a story but as a flash of images—happened when she was nine. She had forgotten to put away the laundry before he came home from his shift. He cornered her in the narrow hallway, backing her against the closet door. She remembers the fabric of his work shirt pressing into her face, the smell of grease and sweat, the way his hand clamped the back of her neck. There are long stretches of that evening she has never been able to retrieve—blank spaces that feel like someone else’s life—but the parts she does remember are vivid, silent photographs: the dark grain of the wooden floor, the sound of her own breathing, the sensation of having no way out. What stays with her most is the certainty that she could have stopped it—if she had been quicker, smarter, stronger. Even now, she believes a different child would have found a way. A normal child. A child who wasn’t already broken inside.

As an adult, Marta threw herself into her work as a community organizer. The long hours, the constant calls, the packing of meeting rooms—all of it served a purpose she didn’t fully admit to herself: keeping her mind too occupied for the images to slip in. She coordinated tenant rights campaigns, led neighborhood forums, and frequently stayed at the office until past midnight. Her colleagues called her dedicated; her partner, a quiet man named Daniel, called her exhausted. She often came home to find him already asleep, and she would stand in the doorway of the bedroom, unable to cross the threshold. Her body had learned that sleep meant dropping her guard. She would lie in the dark, straining to hear footsteps, checking that the door was locked twice, her eyes scanning the room for anything out of place. Some nights she gave up and returned to the living room, propping herself against the wall so that she could see both the front door and the hallway.

In public spaces, Marta had developed an elaborate set of unspoken rules. At the community center where she held weekly meetings, she always arrived early to claim the chair that faced the entrance, its back against the brick wall. If someone else had already taken that seat, she would wait, hovering near the door until they moved, or she would stand through the entire meeting rather than sit exposed. On the street, she frequently glanced over her shoulder, scanning for anyone who might be following her. She knew, intellectually, that she was not being followed, but the act of checking felt necessary—a small ritual that kept the panic at bay. When she caught herself doing it, the shame was immediate: a normal person, a strong person, would not need to look behind them every thirty seconds.

Marta had tried to erase the memory of the abuse altogether. She would tell herself, “It happened to someone else. That girl in the hallway was not me.” And sometimes, when she recalled the event, she felt nothing—a flat, hollow numbness, as though she were watching a stranger’s life on a screen. That numbness frightened her more than the fear itself. It made her feel dead inside, disconnected from everyone around her. When Daniel reached for her at night, she would turn away, not because she was angry but because she did not know how to let him close without also letting the threat close. She had come to believe that she was a fundamentally weak person—someone who had failed to stop her own abuse and was still failing, all these years later, to get over it.

The final push to seek help came after a routine community meeting. A heated dispute over rent control had escalated, and for a moment the room felt tight, the exits blocked by folding chairs and raised voices. Marta had felt her chest close, a sudden certainty that she was trapped, that there was no way out, that she was nine years old again and the door was behind her and someone’s hand was on her neck. She excused herself, walked quickly to the bathroom, and stood with her back to the wall, shaking. When she looked in the mirror, she saw a woman who had built a career out of fighting for other people’s safety but could not secure her own. That night, she told Daniel she needed to talk to someone. What she is most afraid of, as she walks into the therapist’s office for the first time, is that the numbness will turn out to be permanent—that she is, after all, the weak person she has always suspected she is. But she is also hoping, quietly, that there might be a way to stop living behind her own back.
